newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - New European centre to help women fight violence.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - New European centre to help women fight violence.

text.p: Europeans who want policymakers to do more to fight violence against women now have a new weapon -- a centre that will give them statistics to back up their arguments and experts to advise them on strategy.

The European Women's Lobby (EWL), a coalition of women's groups, launched the centre in Brussels this week to highlight issues such as rape, sexual harassment, battering and trafficking in women just ahead of International Women's Day on Saturday (March 8).
"I get more questions on violence than on any other issue," EWL General Secretary Barbara Helfferich told a news conference.
The European Centre on Violence Against Women will collect data, carry out research, promote information exchanges and lobby for change.
Its founders argue that lack of information has hindered efforts to develop effective strategies against violence in Europe.
Groups that work on a local level to provide shelter to victims often have neither the time nor the resources to go beyond their "first-aid" mission, Helfferich said.
"We'll be trying to provide the link between those groups and European policymakers."

The centre will set up an "observatory" of national coordinators from the European Union's 15 countries who will identify all of the legislation, policies, data and research on violence that exists at national level.

They will then identify areas where EU action is needed and recommend activities for the EWL. The centre will also set up a data base to collect information about experts, legislative issues, projects carried out by non-governmental organisations and models of "good practice".
It will also provide the names of women with legal expertise on violence.
HIGHLIGHTING PROBLEM AREAS

Helfferich said the centre, which can draw on the resources of some 2,500 women's groups that are associated with the EWL, would give priority to producing a comparative analysis of national legislation.
That would highlight problem areas -- for example, the countries that do not consider marital rape a crime.
The EWL argues that violence against women is too often seen as an "inevitable" part of society and EU institutions and governments have not done enough to combat the problem.
"By consistently ignoring violence against women, governments have relegated women to the position of second-class citizens," EWL President Gertrud Wartenberg said in a statement.

Helfferich said individual EU commissioners had highlighted violence against women -- for example, Italy's Emma Bonino visited grieving women in Bosnia after the 1995 massacre in Srebrenica, and Sweden's Anita Gradin had given prominence to the issue of women being forced into prostitution.

But she said the EU as a whole did not do enough on the grounds that it did not have jurisdiction. She said the EU treaty needed to be amended to incorporate a set of fundamental human rights, which would cover violence against women.
The EWL and the Women's Rights Committee of the European Parliament are proposing that the Union launch a European Campaign on Violence Against Women whose theme would be "zero tolerance".
The EWL has suggested it be targeted at ordinary people, following the approach taken in the campaign against AIDS.

The lobby is currently funding the centre through its existing funds, which it receives from member organisations and the European Commission. But it is seeking additional corporate sponsors, Helfferich said.

The EWL has made a point of inviting men to join in its campaign. Joachim Lempert, head of the German group Men Against Male Violence, which counsels men who beat women, attended the news conference to launch the new centre.

He said his group, which is working to establish a network of centres for men, tried to make its clients realise that they act violently because they are attempting to place responsibility for their problems on their victims.
"He starts to abuse in situations where he's quite weak and doesn't know where to go," he said.
